asbestos.origin: Asbestos is not one mineral but a commercial and regulatory term for naturally fibrous silicate minerals. They fall into two groups: serpentine, represented by chrysotile, and amphiboles, including crocidolite, amosite, tremolite, anthophyllite and actinolite. Deposits have been mined on every continent except Antarctica. Chrysotile has made up about 95 percent of asbestos used worldwide in recent decades, and about 2 million tons a year were still being used in the mid-2010s, notably in India, China and Russia. This atlas includes asbestos only as historical and safety context and does not recommend handling or processing it.
asbestos.structure: Chrysotile is a magnesium sheet silicate whose layers curl into hollow, scroll-like fibrils, so its fibers are curly and comparatively soluble in lung fluid. Amphiboles are double-chain silicates that form straight, needle-like, highly biopersistent fibers. Both split lengthwise into ever finer fibrils. Disease potency depends on mineral type, fiber length, width and biopersistence: one review links pleural disease to biopersistent fibers thinner than about 0.1 micrometers and longer than about 5 micrometers. Nonfibrous forms of the same minerals exist, and fibrous amphiboles such as winchite and richterite, not historically regulated as asbestos, contaminated vermiculite.
asbestos.process: This atlas does not recommend handling, processing or disturbing asbestos in any form; what follows is historical description only. Mined ore was crushed and milled to free the fibers, which were graded by length, with the longer grades going to textiles. Fibers were carded, often with a carrier fiber such as cotton, spun and woven into cloth, tape, rope and lagging for insulation, gaskets, brake linings and fire-resistant clothing. Textile work was intensely dusty: at a South Carolina plant that processed chrysotile from Quebec, lung cancer risk per unit exposure was about 50 times that in Quebec mining and milling.
asbestos.performance: Asbestos was valued for resistance to heat and chemical breakdown, tensile strength and the ability to be spun and woven, which earned it the label 'miracle mineral'. Those properties do not justify its use: exposure causes asbestosis, lung cancer and malignant mesothelioma, with latencies of up to about 50 years for mesothelioma. Amphiboles are more potent for mesothelioma than chrysotile, but all forms are carcinogenic. Legacy material persists: asbestos-containing brake pads were still found in Hungarian waste streams twenty years after the EU ban. Suspected asbestos textiles, such as old heat-resistant cloth, gloves, rope or gaskets, should be left undisturbed and assessed by qualified professionals.
asbestos.identify: Do not burn, cut, tease apart or sample suspected asbestos. Identification belongs to accredited laboratories. Phase contrast microscopy of air samples counts fibers longer than 5 micrometers, thicker than about 0.25 micrometers and with an aspect ratio of at least 3:1, but cannot tell asbestos from other fibers. Electron microscopy with elemental analysis identifies mineral type and thin fibers, and the EU is moving occupational measurement from optical to electron microscopy by the end of 2029.
asbestos.labeling: Asbestos is regulated as a hazardous substance, not merely labeled as a fiber. The European Union banned asbestos in 2005, and Directive (EU) 2023/2668 lowered the occupational exposure limit from 100,000 to 2,000 fibres per cubic meter when fibres 0.2 to 3 micrometers wide are counted, or 10,000 when thinner fibres are included. In the United States, the EPA issued a ruling in 2024 to ban chrysotile asbestos. More than 50 countries had banned asbestos by the mid-2010s. IARC classifies all forms of asbestos as carcinogenic to humans (Group 1). This is not legal advice.
asbestos.past: Asbestos has been used since antiquity, but at industrial scale only for roughly the last 100 to 150 years. Asbestosis was the first disease identified, and asbestos-caused cancer was recognized in the late 1930s, yet world consumption approached 5 million tons a year in the 1990s. Controversies over the relative hazards of fiber types and sizes, some described by researchers as manufactured, slowed bans. A 2018 estimate put deaths caused by asbestos at about 255,000 a year, about 233,000 of them from work exposure, borne by miners, textile workers, insulators and builders. Legacy asbestos in buildings, vehicles and waste keeps the hazard current.
